My study topics include multidimensional data analysis, statistical modeling and neural networks. I have personal interest in all kinds of data that relate to geography, maps and transportation infrastructure (motorways, train networks, plane routes).

title: Fewer Infections, More Harm? The Paradox of Germany’s Hospital Infections
text:
Scrubbing up before surgery is one of medicine’s oldest rituals, and one of its most effective. Before every operation, surgeons spend minutes washing their hands and forearms, because a single contaminated hand can carry bacteria straight into a patient’s body during the procedure.
Even so, hospitals remain a place where people catch infections. On any given day, about one in 18 patients in a European hospital has at least one infection acquired during their stay (ECDC, 2013). These are called healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), infections that develop in hospital and are unrelated to the reason for admission. A procedure can go perfectly, and the patient can still develop a urinary tract infection from a catheter a few days later. In Germany, an estimated 20 to 30% of HAIs are preventable (Gastmeier et al., 2010), but prevention resources are limited, so knowing which infections cause the most harm matters as much as knowing how many there are.
Germany is a particularly interesting case: per hospitalised patient, its infection rate is below the European average; across the whole population however, Germans lose more years of healthy life to HAIs than the European average. This post looks at three questions: how large the burden of HAIs in Germany is, which infections drive it, and how a lower risk per patient can still produce a higher burden overall.

title: Fewer Infections, More Harm? The Paradox of Germany’s Hospital Infections
section: Everything went right. So what went wrong?
text:
Everything went right. So what went wrong?
Imagine your mother goes in for a knee replacement. The surgeons scrub up, the operation goes well, and then on day four she develops a urinary tract infection from her catheter. Nobody made an obvious mistake. This is a healthcare-associated infection (HAI): an infection caught because of a hospital stay. In Germany, 20 to 30% of them are thought to be preventable (Zacher et al., 2019).
Germany poses a puzzle. A German hospital patient is less likely to have one of these infections than the average European patient, yet across the whole population, Germans lose more healthy life to them. So:

How big is the problem?
How can fewer infections per patient mean a bigger burden overall?

Fewer Infections, More Harm? The Paradox of Germany’s Hospital Infections
text:
So, is it the hygiene?
Mostly not. Hospital infections are a large problem in Germany: they cost the country more healthy years than flu, Salmonella, hepatitis B and measles combined. The most common infections are not the most dangerous ones, so the infections to focus on are not necessarily the ones that turn up most often. And Germany’s gap with Europe is mostly about how many people go into hospital, not how clean those hospitals are: German hospitals infect a smaller share of their patients than the European average, but because so many more Germans pass through them each year, the total toll is higher.
That points to two ways of reducing the burden: keep improving infection control, so that the scrubbing ritual from the opening photo keeps doing its job, and avoid hospital stays that are not really needed (Zacher et al., 2019). The good news is that BHAI is free and openly available, so any country with survey data can now run the same check on its own hospitals, and track whether things are getting better.

title: Fewer Infections, More Harm? The Paradox of Germany’s Hospital Infections
section: The most common infection isn’t the most dangerous
text:
The most common infection isn’t the most dangerous
Not all hospital infections are equal. Figure 1 compares how many people catch each infection with how many die from it. Urinary tract infections are by far the most common, but they are usually mild and easy to treat. Bloodstream infections and C. difficile, a severe gut infection often triggered by antibiotics, are much rarer, yet they are far more likely to kill: hover over the bars to see what share of infected patients die from each one. This is exactly why counting infections is not enough; a hospital that only tracked the most frequent infections would be focusing on the wrong problem.








Figure 1: People infected (left) and deaths (right) in Germany in one year, by type of hospital infection. Hover over a bar to see the share of infected patients who die.

title: Fewer Infections, More Harm? The Paradox of Germany’s Hospital Infections
text:
Germany compared to Europe
So far, these numbers only describe Germany. Compared with the European average, and adjusting for population size, Germany has around 27% more hospital infections, 34% more deaths from them, and 7% more healthy years lost. Figure 2 shows that the gap is not spread evenly across infection types: most of Germany’s extra burden comes from urinary tract and C. difficile infections, while hospital pneumonia is actually less of a burden in Germany than in the rest of Europe (Zacher et al., 2019). In other words, Germany is not simply doing worse across the board.








Figure 2: Healthy years lost per 100,000 people by type of hospital infection, Germany vs the EU/EEA average (2011–2012). Thin lines show the range the true value most likely falls in.

title: Fewer Infections, More Harm? The Paradox of Germany’s Hospital Infections
text:
So, was Semmelweis right?
Yes, but hygiene is only half of the story. Hospital infections are a large problem in Germany: they cost the country more healthy years than flu, Salmonella, hepatitis B and measles combined. The most common infections are not the most dangerous ones, so the infections to focus on are not necessarily the ones that turn up most often. And Germany’s gap with Europe is mostly about how many people go into hospital, not how clean those hospitals are: German hospitals infect a smaller share of their patients than the European average, but because so many more Germans pass through them each year, the total toll is higher.
That points to two ways of reducing the burden: keep improving infection control, as Semmelweis did, and avoid hospital stays that are not really needed (Zacher et al., 2019). The good news is that BHAI is free and openly available, so any country with survey data can now run the same check on its own hospitals, and track whether things are getting better.
